newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chubais, on regional tour, says Russian cash tight.
newsitem.headline: Chubais, on regional tour, says Russian cash tight.

text.p: Economic reform chief Anatoly Chubais, lobbying for backing in far-flung parts of the Russian Federation, said on Thursday he welcomed advice from regional governors, but warned them money was in short supply.
"Don't seek a slice of the budget cake," Chubais, one of two Russian First Deputy Prime Ministers, told local leaders in the diamond centre of Yakutia, six time zones east of Moscow.
Chubais arrived in the remote settlement of Mirny from the regional capital Yakutsk after a tour which also took him to a meeting of Siberian leaders in the industrial city of Krasnoyarsk.
During the trip he highlighted the need for discussions with regional leaders on Russia's 1998 budget plan, and said the government had time to take their views into consideration.
"Suggestions from the governors look absolutely reasonable to me and we will work on them," he said.
Chubais, once the mastermind of Russia's bold privatisation campaign, was brought back into the government in March to kick-start a stalled programme of economic reforms.
Assisted by anti-corruption crusader Boris Nemtsov, he has launched new initiatives to rein in public spending and promised to create Russia's first "realistic budget" since reforms began.
A sequestration programme to be presented to parliament next week envisages slashing spending by 108 trillion roubles ($18.7 billion).

But the ambitious economist will have his work cut out to persuade regional bosses and conservative parliamentarians to approve the deep and painful spending cuts, which the government says will compensate for a pitifully low tax take.
"I do not understand why this sequestration is needed," Krasnoyarsk Governor Valery Zubov told the meeting there. "I cannot see it having political, economic, financial or legal sense."

Gennady Seleznyov, speaker of the communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament, said in Moscow on Thursday that parliament might make a counter-proposal, suggesting that the government print money to deal with the budget crisis.

"These would be the roubles tied to the economy. They should not be converted in dollars and leave the country... Enterprises will get funds and people will receive wages they have been waiting for for four or five months," Seleznyov said.
Ministers and the central bank have already said they will not support a plan for higher cash emission, and central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin warned it would trigger hyperinflation.

Russian prices rose one percent in April, still high by the standards of Western countries, but negligible compared to the double-digit monthly inflation seen in the early years of Russia's economic reform programme.

Seleznyov also said the Duma might be ready to compromise on lower spending cuts than those suggested by the government, but his suggested cuts of 30 trillion roubles are unlikely to meet government approval.
Chubais said in Krarsnoyarsk that economic growth was the way to resolve problems with the budget, with non-payments and with falling living standards.
"The main task of the government must be to ensure that 1998 becomes the year of growth," he said. ($ = 5761 Russian Roubles)
